Thyroid Disorders: Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism is a condition characterized by underproduction of thyroid hormones by the thyroid gland, leading to a decrease in metabolic rate. The normal range for TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) is 0.4-4.5 μU/mL, and for free T4 (FT4) is 0.8-1.8 ng/dL. Hypothyroidism can be classified into two main types: primary and secondary.

Definition

Hypothyroidism is defined as a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce sufficient thyroid hormones, namely triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4), to meet the body's needs. This can be due to a problem with the thyroid gland itself (primary hypothyroidism) or a problem with the pituitary gland or hypothalamus (secondary hypothyroidism).

Types/Classification

There are several types of hypothyroidism, including:

  • Primary hypothyroidism: This is the most common type, accounting for about 90% of cases. It is caused by a problem with the thyroid gland itself, such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, radiation therapy, or surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
  • Secondary hypothyroidism: This type is caused by a problem with the pituitary gland, which is responsible for producing TSH. This can be due to a tumor, injury, or infection.
  • Tertiary hypothyroidism: This is a rare type of hypothyroidism caused by a problem with the hypothalamus, which is responsible for producing TRH (Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone).

Mechanism/Pathophysiology

The mechanism of hypothyroidism involves a decrease in the production of thyroid hormones, which are essential for metabolic rate, growth and development, and energy production. The decrease in thyroid hormones leads to a decrease in basal metabolic rate, resulting in weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance.

Clinical Features

The clinical features of hypothyroidism include:

  • Weight gain
  • Fatigue
  • Cold intolerance
  • Dry skin
  • Hair loss
  • Constipation
  • Depression
  • Memory loss

A helpful mnemonic to remember the symptoms of hypothyroidism is COLD: C - constipation, O - obesity, L - lassitude (fatigue), D - dry skin.

Management

The management of hypothyroidism involves thyroid hormone replacement therapy. The goal of treatment is to restore normal thyroid hormone levels and alleviate symptoms. The most commonly used medication is levothyroxine (T4), which is taken orally. The usual starting dose is 50-100 μg/day, and the dose is adjusted based on TSH levels.

Nursing Care

Nursing care for patients with hypothyroidism includes:

  • Monitoring of TSH levels
  • Administration of thyroid hormone replacement therapy
  • Education on medication adherence
  • Monitoring for signs of overdose or underdose
  • Encouragement of a healthy lifestyle, including a balanced diet and regular exercise

Key Points

Key points to remember about hypothyroidism include:

  • Primary hypothyroidism is the most common type, accounting for about 90% of cases.
  • TSH levels are used to diagnose and monitor hypothyroidism.
  • Levothyroxine (T4) is the most commonly used medication for thyroid hormone replacement therapy.
  • Normal TSH levels are between 0.4-4.5 μU/mL.
  • Normal FT4 levels are between 0.8-1.8 ng/dL.

A helpful mnemonic to remember the key points is THYROID: T - TSH levels, H - hypothyroidism, Y - years of treatment, R - replacement therapy, O - ongoing monitoring, I - individualized treatment, D - diet and exercise.
